script.opening: (Frustrated, a little breathless, inhaler in hand.) "Doctor, these inhalers just aren't doing anything any more — I'm as breathless as ever and I keep getting chest infections. Can you give me something stronger? Maybe one of those triple inhalers I've read about. I feel like I'm going backwards."

facts.text: "I have to stop more than I used to when I'm out walking. It's getting me down." Stops after 100 metres on the flat (MRC 3). Can still dress and wash herself.

"More than once this year, I know that. I'd have to check about hospital." If asked to think: two courses of steroids and antibiotics from the surgery this year (January and May), no hospital admission.

If asked to show: "Like this…" — opens the dry-powder inhaler, doesn't breathe out first, takes a short, gentle sniff of a breath, no breath-hold, breathes out straight away. "Nobody's ever watched me do it."
"Most days. Sometimes I forget if I'm feeling alright." Uses her blue inhaler 3–4 times a day.
"No, nothing like that" — no blood in sputum, no weight loss, no chest pain, no ankle swelling, no waking breathless at night.

COPD diagnosed 5 years ago with spirometry. Ex-smoker — stopped 3 years ago (35 pack-years). No childhood asthma, no hay fever or eczema. High blood pressure (amlodipine). Never offered pulmonary rehab. Flu jab yes; not sure about pneumonia or RSV jabs. No allergies.
Widowed, lives alone in a first-floor flat (stairs). Daughter does her big shop. Used to love walking to the park.

Frustrated: "I feel like I'm going backwards." If asked what worries her: "Ending up stuck indoors. Not being able to manage on my own." Sceptical about rehab: "Exercise? I can barely walk." — then "Alright, I'll try it" if it's explained as supervised and built for people like her. Pleased by the plan: "That feels like a proper plan." If simply given a new inhaler without checking, accept happily (the trap).

ice.ideas: "The inhalers have stopped working — I need a stronger one, like the triple."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of losing her independence and being stuck indoors; worn down by repeated chest infections.

cues: "Nobody's ever watched me do it." — technique has never been checked.
"I feel like I'm going backwards." — the fear to explore.

checkpoints.text: Checks INHALER TECHNIQUE (asks the patient to demonstrate) and corrects it — recognising poor technique as the commonest reason inhalers "stop working" — and considers a spacer/better-matched device before escalating

Reviews ADHERENCE, confirms a spirometry-based diagnosis, looks for asthmatic features (NG115: prior asthma/atopy, higher eosinophils, FEV1 or PEF variability), and screens treatable contributors (smoking/exposure, heart failure, anaemia, anxiety, deconditioning, weight)

Optimises NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL care — refers to PULMONARY REHABILITATION (MRC dyspnoea ≥3/functionally limited), checks vaccinations against UKHSA Green Book eligibility, reinforces cessation, and provides a self-management plan/rescue pack — before or alongside any escalation

Applies NICE NG115 escalation LOGIC: on LABA+LAMA with optimised basics, considers adding an INHALED CORTICOSTEROID (triple therapy) after 1 severe (hospital) or 2 moderate exacerbations in a year, or a 3-month trial for symptoms affecting quality of life with a return to LABA+LAMA if no improvement — asthmatic features and eosinophils inform, with no set cut-off — and knows the specialist options beyond it (azithromycin, roflumilast, dupilumab per TA1142)

Counsels the ICS trade-off (reduced exacerbations vs increased PNEUMONIA risk), uses a combination inhaler for adherence, and plans to review benefit (stop ICS if no benefit) — not "stronger by default"
Validates the frustration and the fear of "going backwards", and reframes the plan around fixable basics and rehab rather than dismissing her request
Explains the technique/escalation reasoning clearly, checks understanding (teach-back of inhaler technique), and supports adherence

Safety-nets and follows up: review after optimisation/rehab, exacerbation action plan, NICE NG12 lung awareness if red flags (haemoptysis, weight loss), and a clear escalation/de-escalation plan with review of any ICS benefit — fixing the basics, not reflexive escalation

worked.txt: "I can hear how frustrating this is, and ‘going backwards’ is a horrible feeling. Before I just add a stronger inhaler — which I will if it’s the right thing — let me check a few things that very often make the difference, because a new inhaler that’s used the same way may not help."

"Could you show me exactly how you take your inhaler, as if I weren’t here? … Ah — I can see the breath and the press aren’t quite together. That’s incredibly common, and it means a lot of the medicine isn’t reaching your lungs. Let me show you, and a spacer might help too."

"A few other things: are you managing to take it every day? Have you had your flu jab this year and your one-off pneumonia jab? I’ll also check whether you’re eligible for this season’s COVID booster. And the single most effective treatment for breathlessness that isn’t a drug at all is pulmonary rehab — a supervised exercise-and-education programme. I’d really like to refer you."

"If we’ve sorted technique and you’re still breathless or getting lots of flares, then yes — adding a third medicine, a steroid inhaler, makes sense if you’ve had two flare-ups needing treatment, or one hospital stay, in the past year, or as a three-month trial for your breathlessness that we stop if it doesn’t help. I’ll also check a blood count, because a raised level of one type of white cell can point to who benefits most."

"Being straight: that steroid inhaler can cut down flares, but it slightly raises the risk of pneumonia, so it’s a considered choice, not just ‘stronger’. We’ll use one combined inhaler to keep it simple, and review whether it’s actually helping."

"So: fix the technique, get you onto pulmonary rehab and up to date with jabs, and review in a few weeks — escalating then if needed. If you cough up blood or lose weight, tell me. And let’s make sure you’ve a rescue plan for flares."

f.learning: When a COPD patient says their inhalers "aren’t working" and asks for "something stronger", resist reflexive escalation and CHECK THE BASICS first. The commonest reason for apparent inhaler failure is poor TECHNIQUE — ask the patient to demonstrate, correct critical errors (coordination with MDIs, inspiratory effort with dry-powder devices, breath-holding), consider a spacer or a better-matched device, and re-check; this alone often transforms control. Also review ADHERENCE, confirm a spirometry-based diagnosis (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7), look for asthmatic features (NICE NG115), and screen treatable contributors (ongoing smoking/exposure, heart failure, anaemia, anxiety, deconditioning, weight). Optimise NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL care, which is frequently more impactful than escalation: refer for PULMONARY REHABILITATION (strong evidence for breathlessness and quality of life; offer if MRC dyspnoea ≥3/functionally limited), ensure vaccinations (influenza and pneumococcal, and COVID-19 only if she meets current UKHSA Green Book eligibility), reinforce cessation, and provide a self-management plan with a rescue pack. Only then apply NICE NG115 escalation LOGIC: on LABA+LAMA with optimised basics, consider adding an INHALED CORTICOSTEROID (triple therapy) after 1 severe exacerbation needing hospital or 2 moderate exacerbations within a year, or as a 3-month trial for day-to-day symptoms affecting quality of life with a return to LABA+LAMA if there is no improvement (asthmatic features, including a higher blood eosinophil count, inform the choice, but NG115 sets no cut-off) — counselling the trade-off that ICS reduces exacerbations in the right patient but raises PNEUMONIA risk, using a single combination inhaler for adherence, and reviewing benefit (stopping ICS if none); beyond triple therapy, specialist options include azithromycin prophylaxis, roflumilast (NICE TA461) and, since 2026, dupilumab for raised eosinophils (NICE TA1142). Validate the patient’s frustration and fear of decline, reframe around fixable basics and rehab, keep NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) lung awareness for red flags, and follow up — reasoned care, not "stronger by default".

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG115 (COPD in over 16s, 2018, updated 2019; reviewed July 2026 with a new biological-therapy section) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE TA1142 (dupilumab, March 2026) and NICE TA1166 (mepolizumab, June 2026) for uncontrolled COPD with raised blood eosinophils) · [4] UKHSA Green Book
knowledge.summary: Before escalating, check technique, adherence, the diagnosis and the non-drug treatments, especially pulmonary rehabilitation. Then apply the NG115 step to triple therapy on its stated criteria, with the pneumonia trade-off discussed and a planned review.

points.t: NICE NG115 [1]: check inhaler technique and adherence before starting or changing inhaled therapy, and at each review. Ask her to demonstrate; consider a spacer or a better-matched device.

Confirm the record holds post-bronchodilator spirometry (FEV1/FVC below 0.7). Look for asthmatic features (NICE NG115 [1]: previous asthma or atopy, higher blood eosinophil count, FEV1 variation of at least 400 ml, diurnal PEF variation of at least 20%) and for heart failure, anaemia, anxiety or depression, and deconditioning.

NICE NG115 [1]: offer pulmonary rehabilitation to people who see themselves as functionally disabled by COPD (usually MRC grade 3 and above). It improves breathlessness, exercise capacity and quality of life.

NICE NG115 [1], on LABA+LAMA: consider LABA+LAMA+ICS after a severe exacerbation (needing hospital) or 2 moderate exacerbations within a year. If day-to-day symptoms still affect quality of life, consider a 3-month trial of LABA+LAMA+ICS and return to LABA+LAMA if there is no improvement.
NICE NG115 [1]: discuss and document the increased risk of pneumonia with inhaled corticosteroids. A single combined inhaler is simpler to use; review the benefit.

Specialist options for continued exacerbations include azithromycin prophylaxis in non-smokers after optimisation (NICE NG115 [1], with CT, sputum culture, ECG and LFT checks first) and, since 2026, biological therapy: dupilumab per NICE TA1142 or mepolizumab per NICE TA1166 [2] for uncontrolled COPD with raised blood eosinophils despite maximal inhaled therapy.

Annual influenza vaccination and a one-off pneumococcal vaccine; COVID-19 and RSV per current UKHSA Green Book [4] eligibility. NICE NG12 [3]: ever-smokers aged 40 and over with an unexplained symptom such as cough, breathlessness, weight loss or chest pain need an urgent chest X-ray; a change from her usual pattern should not be put down to COPD.

Daily activity, independence, and the effect of breathlessness on mood and life at home.
Technique demonstration, adherence, spirometry in the record, FBC with eosinophils, exacerbation count.
Poor technique and adherence, deconditioning, asthmatic features, heart failure, anaemia, anxiety, lung cancer.
Asked about haemoptysis, weight loss, oedema and orthopnoea; NICE NG12 low threshold for ever-smokers.
Explained inadequate control of COPD with fixable contributors, and where triple therapy fits.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Technique and adherence fixed; pulmonary rehab; triple therapy on NG115 criteria with pneumonia trade-off and review.
Vaccinations, rescue-pack plan, and screening of cardiac, haematological and mood contributors.
999 and red-flag symptoms named; nurse technique check; review in 4 to 6 weeks.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “going backwards” and the missed doses when well.
Idea (inhalers have stopped working), concern (losing independence), expectation (triple inhaler).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — fear of losing her independence and being stuck indoors; worn down by repeated chest infections — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Coralie, I’m Dr Hughes. I understand your breathing’s been getting you down. Tell me about it.

These inhalers just aren’t doing anything any more. I’m as breathless as ever and I keep getting chest infections. Can I have something stronger — one of those triple inhalers I’ve read about? I feel like I’m going backwards.

That sounds really frustrating, and I’m glad you’ve looked into it. Triple inhalers are definitely on the table. Can we look at how things are going first, then decide together what’s most likely to help?
model.why: Validates, keeps her option open and agrees an agenda

model.text: Alright.
What can’t you do now that you want to be able to do?
model.why: Explores the impact in her terms

model.text: I have to stop more than I used to when I’m out walking. It’s getting me down.
And the chest infections — how many have needed steroids or antibiotics in the last year, and did any put you in hospital?
model.why: Counts exacerbations for the NG115 escalation criteria

model.text: More than once this year, I know that. I’d have to check about hospital.
I can check your record for that. Could you get your inhaler and show me exactly how you take it, as if I weren’t here?
Like this…

Thank you. I can see a couple of things we can improve in how you breathe in with it — that’s really common, and it means less medicine reaches your lungs. Let me show you, and I’ll ask the nurse to check it with you in person.
Nobody’s ever watched me do it.
Then this is worth doing. Honestly, how many days a week do you manage to use it?
Most days. Sometimes I forget if I’m feeling alright.
Thanks for being honest. Any coughing up blood, weight loss, ankle swelling or needing more pillows at night?
model.why: Screens NICE NG12 red flags and heart failure

model.text: No, nothing like that.
You said you feel like you’re going backwards. What worries you most about that?
Ending up stuck indoors. Not being able to manage on my own.
That’s a very real worry, and it’s exactly what I want to help you avoid. What were you hoping for from today?
model.why: Validates the fear and elicits expectations

model.text: A stronger inhaler, I suppose.

Here’s what I think. Some of this is likely the technique and missed days — a stronger inhaler taken the same way often disappoints. The treatment with the best evidence for breathlessness isn’t a drug at all: pulmonary rehabilitation, a supervised exercise and education course.
model.why: Explains basics and offers pulmonary rehab

model.text: Exercise? I can barely walk.
It’s designed for exactly that, with people at your level, and most people find they can do more afterwards. It’s one of the best ways to stay independent.
model.why: Links rehab to her concern about independence

model.text: Alright, I’ll try it.

About the triple inhaler: it adds a steroid inhaler. With repeated flares it’s a reasonable step, and it can cut down flares. The trade-off is a slightly higher risk of pneumonia, so I want to be sure you’d benefit.
model.why: NG115 escalation logic and ICS pneumonia trade-off

model.text: So here’s my suggestion. Today: sort the technique, a reminder to use it daily, and a blood count, which includes a type of white cell that helps us judge whether a steroid inhaler is likely to help. I’ll check your spirometry and flare history in the record, and refer you to pulmonary rehab.
model.why: Shared plan: technique, FBC with eosinophils, record check, rehab

model.text: If your record shows the flares meet the threshold, I’ll switch you to a single triple inhaler now rather than make you wait. If not, we review in a few weeks, and if you’re still struggling we try triple for three months and go back if it doesn’t help. Does that feel fair?
Yes. That feels like a proper plan.
And your flu and pneumonia jabs — I’ll check they’re up to date, and whether you’re due any others. I’ll also update your rescue-pack plan so you can start treatment quickly.
If you get much more breathless, drowsy or confused, call 999. If you cough up blood, lose weight without trying, or your cough changes, tell me — I wouldn’t want that put down to your COPD.
model.why: Specific safety-net including NICE NG12 awareness

model.text: Okay.
Can you tell me the plan back?
Fix how I take it, use it every day, blood test, rehab, jabs, and a triple inhaler if my record shows the flares — otherwise review in a few weeks.
Exactly. The nurse will check your technique in person, and I’ll see you in four to six weeks.

social.t: Breathlessness restricts activity, which leads to deconditioning, isolation and low mood. Pulmonary rehabilitation addresses all three.
Dexterity, device type, cost of prescriptions and remembering doses all affect adherence; a single combined inhaler helps.

legal.t: If breathlessness limits her mobility, she may be eligible for a Blue Badge or disability benefits; signpost where appropriate.

professional.t: NICE NG197 (shared decision making, 2021): discuss benefits and risks, including the ICS pneumonia risk, and document the discussion.
Check technique at every review. The practice nurse or community pharmacist (New Medicine Service when a new inhaler starts) can reinforce it.

community.t: Pulmonary rehabilitation, Asthma + Lung UK information and Breathe Easy support groups.

redFlags: Haemoptysis, weight loss or change in cough in an ex-smoker
Breathlessness at rest, drowsiness or confusion
psychosocial: What she can no longer do, and her fear of losing independence
ice: Concern: going backwards and losing independence

playbook.diagnosis: “Your COPD isn’t as well controlled as it could be. Part of that is likely how the inhaler is taken and missed days, and part is the flares. There’s a lot we can improve before and alongside a new inhaler.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “An inhaler is like a key: the right key only works if you turn it the right way. Let’s get the turning right, and build up your fitness, and then see if you need a different key.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you’re frightened of being stuck indoors. Pulmonary rehab is one of the best ways to keep you getting out, and that’s why I’m keen on it.”
management.psychosocial: Normalise technique errors; negotiate daily use; frame rehab around independence.
sharedPlan: Correct technique; nurse check in person; daily use
Pulmonary rehabilitation referral; vaccinations; rescue-pack plan
FBC and record check; LABA+LAMA+ICS on NG115 criteria, or a 3-month trial for persistent symptoms, with pneumonia risk documented
safetyNet: 999: breathless at rest, drowsy or confused
Report haemoptysis, weight loss or change in cough; review in 4 to 6 weeks

pitfalls.intro: This station is passed by candidates who watch the patient use her inhaler. It is failed by those who escalate on request, or who refuse and leave her feeling unheard.

items.fail: Switching to a triple inhaler without watching her use the current one.
items.why: NICE NG115 asks for a technique and adherence check before any change. “Management not in line with guidance.”
items.fix: “Could you show me exactly how you take it?” — then correct and teach back.

items.why: It is one of the most effective treatments for breathlessness; omitting it is a Tasks gap.
items.fix: Offer it early and link it to what she wants back.

items.fail: Adding ICS “because she wants stronger”, with no pneumonia discussion or review plan.
items.why: NICE NG115 sets exacerbation criteria, a 3-month trial for symptoms, and asks for the pneumonia risk to be discussed and documented.
items.fix: State the criteria and the trade-off, and set a review date.

items.fail: “You just need to use it properly.”
items.why: Blame reads as dismissive and loses Relating marks.
items.fix: “That’s really common — a couple of small changes could help a lot.”

items.fail: Missing “I feel like I’m going backwards.”
items.why: “Does not explore the patient’s concerns.” Her fear of losing independence is the hinge of the plan.
items.fix: “What worries you most about going backwards?”

items.fail: A plan that ends with “we’ll see how you get on”.
items.why: No defined review or escalation point leaves her where she started.
items.fix: A conditional plan with a date: triple now if criteria met, otherwise review in 4 to 6 weeks.

timeMap.d: Acknowledge frustration and her research. Keep triple therapy on the table.
Impact, exacerbation count, technique demonstration, adherence, red flags and heart failure screen.
“Going backwards” = fear of losing independence. Name it.
Technique and adherence, pulmonary rehab, then NG115 triple-therapy criteria with the pneumonia trade-off. FBC, record check, vaccines, rescue plan.
999 signs, NICE NG12 red flags, teach-back, nurse technique check, review in 4 to 6 weeks.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes a triple inhaler on request without watching her use her current one; no pulmonary rehab; no mention of pneumonia risk; or refuses outright and leaves her feeling dismissed.
wordPics.pass: Checks technique and adherence, refers to pulmonary rehab, explains when triple therapy is appropriate with the pneumonia risk, and arranges review.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: applies the exact NG115 criteria (exacerbation count, 3-month trial for symptoms), links rehab to her fear of losing independence, checks the record for spirometry and asthmatic features, uses teach-back for technique, and sets a conditional plan so she is not made to wait unnecessarily.

avoid.dont: “I’ll just switch you to the triple inhaler.”
avoid.instead: “Could you show me how you take your current one first?”
avoid.why: Escalating without a technique check is the core failure in this station.

avoid.dont: “You don’t need a stronger inhaler, you need to use this one properly.”
avoid.instead: “A couple of small changes in how you breathe in could make a real difference — that’s very common.”
avoid.why: Blame damages the relationship; normalising errors keeps her engaged.

avoid.dont: “The steroid inhaler is stronger, so it should work better.”
avoid.instead: “It can cut down flares, but it slightly raises the risk of pneumonia, so we’ll check it’s helping.”
avoid.why: NICE NG115 asks you to discuss and document the pneumonia risk.

SCA_STEM.recent: Persistent breathlessness and repeated chest infections despite LABA/LAMA. Asking for “something stronger”.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video COPD review: “My inhalers just aren’t working any more.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG115 (COPD in over 16s, 2018, updated 2019; reviewed July 2026 with a new biological-therapy section) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE TA1142 (dupilumab, March 2026) and NICE TA1166 (mepolizumab, June 2026) for uncontrolled COPD with raised blood eosinophils) · [4] UKHSA Green Book
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Before escalating, check technique, adherence, the diagnosis and the non-drug treatments, especially pulmonary rehabilitation. Then apply the NG115 step to triple therapy on its stated criteria, with the pneumonia trade-off discussed and a planned review.

points.t: NICE NG115 [1]: check inhaler technique and adherence before starting or changing inhaled therapy, and at each review. Ask her to demonstrate; consider a spacer or a better-matched device.

Confirm the record holds post-bronchodilator spirometry (FEV1/FVC below 0.7). Look for asthmatic features (NICE NG115 [1]: previous asthma or atopy, higher blood eosinophil count, FEV1 variation of at least 400 ml, diurnal PEF variation of at least 20%) and for heart failure, anaemia, anxiety or depression, and deconditioning.

NICE NG115 [1]: offer pulmonary rehabilitation to people who see themselves as functionally disabled by COPD (usually MRC grade 3 and above). It improves breathlessness, exercise capacity and quality of life.

NICE NG115 [1], on LABA+LAMA: consider LABA+LAMA+ICS after a severe exacerbation (needing hospital) or 2 moderate exacerbations within a year. If day-to-day symptoms still affect quality of life, consider a 3-month trial of LABA+LAMA+ICS and return to LABA+LAMA if there is no improvement.
NICE NG115 [1]: discuss and document the increased risk of pneumonia with inhaled corticosteroids. A single combined inhaler is simpler to use; review the benefit.

Specialist options for continued exacerbations include azithromycin prophylaxis in non-smokers after optimisation (NICE NG115 [1], with CT, sputum culture, ECG and LFT checks first) and, since 2026, biological therapy: dupilumab per NICE TA1142 or mepolizumab per NICE TA1166 [2] for uncontrolled COPD with raised blood eosinophils despite maximal inhaled therapy.

Annual influenza vaccination and a one-off pneumococcal vaccine; COVID-19 and RSV per current UKHSA Green Book [4] eligibility. NICE NG12 [3]: ever-smokers aged 40 and over with an unexplained symptom such as cough, breathlessness, weight loss or chest pain need an urgent chest X-ray; a change from her usual pattern should not be put down to COPD.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; acknowledged frustration and her research without dismissing the request.
Daily activity, independence, and the effect of breathlessness on mood and life at home.
Picked up “going backwards” and the missed doses when well.
Idea (inhalers have stopped working), concern (losing independence), expectation (triple inhaler).
Technique demonstration, adherence, spirometry in the record, FBC with eosinophils, exacerbation count.
Poor technique and adherence, deconditioning, asthmatic features, heart failure, anaemia, anxiety, lung cancer.
Asked about haemoptysis, weight loss, oedema and orthopnoea; NICE NG12 low threshold for ever-smokers.
Explained inadequate control of COPD with fixable contributors, and where triple therapy fits.
Technique and adherence fixed; pulmonary rehab; triple therapy on NG115 criteria with pneumonia trade-off and review.
Vaccinations, rescue-pack plan, and screening of cardiac, haematological and mood contributors.
999 and red-flag symptoms named; nurse technique check; review in 4 to 6 weeks.

social.t: Breathlessness restricts activity, which leads to deconditioning, isolation and low mood. Pulmonary rehabilitation addresses all three.
Dexterity, device type, cost of prescriptions and remembering doses all affect adherence; a single combined inhaler helps.

legal.t: If breathlessness limits her mobility, she may be eligible for a Blue Badge or disability benefits; signpost where appropriate.

professional.t: NICE NG197 (shared decision making, 2021): discuss benefits and risks, including the ICS pneumonia risk, and document the discussion.
Check technique at every review. The practice nurse or community pharmacist (New Medicine Service when a new inhaler starts) can reinforce it.

community.t: Pulmonary rehabilitation, Asthma + Lung UK information and Breathe Easy support groups.

redFlags: Haemoptysis, weight loss or change in cough in an ex-smoker
Breathlessness at rest, drowsiness or confusion
psychosocial: What she can no longer do, and her fear of losing independence
ice: Concern: going backwards and losing independence

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Your COPD isn’t as well controlled as it could be. Part of that is likely how the inhaler is taken and missed days, and part is the flares. There’s a lot we can improve before and alongside a new inhaler.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “An inhaler is like a key: the right key only works if you turn it the right way. Let’s get the turning right, and build up your fitness, and then see if you need a different key.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you’re frightened of being stuck indoors. Pulmonary rehab is one of the best ways to keep you getting out, and that’s why I’m keen on it.”
management.psychosocial: Normalise technique errors; negotiate daily use; frame rehab around independence.
sharedPlan: Correct technique; nurse check in person; daily use
Pulmonary rehabilitation referral; vaccinations; rescue-pack plan
FBC and record check; LABA+LAMA+ICS on NG115 criteria, or a 3-month trial for persistent symptoms, with pneumonia risk documented
safetyNet: 999: breathless at rest, drowsy or confused
Report haemoptysis, weight loss or change in cough; review in 4 to 6 weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is passed by candidates who watch the patient use her inhaler. It is failed by those who escalate on request, or who refuse and leave her feeling unheard.

items.fail: Switching to a triple inhaler without watching her use the current one.
items.why: NICE NG115 asks for a technique and adherence check before any change. “Management not in line with guidance.”
items.fix: “Could you show me exactly how you take it?” — then correct and teach back.

items.why: It is one of the most effective treatments for breathlessness; omitting it is a Tasks gap.
items.fix: Offer it early and link it to what she wants back.

items.fail: Adding ICS “because she wants stronger”, with no pneumonia discussion or review plan.
items.why: NICE NG115 sets exacerbation criteria, a 3-month trial for symptoms, and asks for the pneumonia risk to be discussed and documented.
items.fix: State the criteria and the trade-off, and set a review date.

items.fail: “You just need to use it properly.”
items.why: Blame reads as dismissive and loses Relating marks.
items.fix: “That’s really common — a couple of small changes could help a lot.”

items.fail: Missing “I feel like I’m going backwards.”
items.why: “Does not explore the patient’s concerns.” Her fear of losing independence is the hinge of the plan.
items.fix: “What worries you most about going backwards?”

items.fail: A plan that ends with “we’ll see how you get on”.
items.why: No defined review or escalation point leaves her where she started.
items.fix: A conditional plan with a date: triple now if criteria met, otherwise review in 4 to 6 weeks.
